title: Perfect Spiral M74
caption: The spiral galaxy M74, imaged by the Gemini North telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This color picture shows NGC 628, better known as M74, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Pisces, nicknamed the Perfect Spiral in its release title. It was taken on Mauna Kea, Hawaiʻi, with the 8.1-meter Gemini North telescope, using the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph, or GMOS, an instrument that had just been commissioned.

To make the color image, three separate pictures were combined as the red, green and blue layers of a composite. The observations were made on 13 and 14 August 2001, and the field covers 5.7 by 5.4 arcminutes.

A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust whose arms wind out from a bright central region. The arms stand out because they are where gas collects and young stars form. Galaxies like M74, seen with their arms laid out clearly, are useful for studying how that spiral pattern is organized.

understand.summary: GMOS on Gemini North imaged M74 in visible and near-infrared light through g, r and i filters, combined into a red, green and blue composite. Which filter went to which color is not stated.
understand.eye: The i filter reaches into near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and an 8-meter mirror gathers far more light than a human eye.

behind.people: See full credit: International Gemini Observatory/GMOS Commissioning Team
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Although GMOS is a spectrograph, able to split light from many objects into spectra at once, it can also take direct images, as it did here during its commissioning, the period when a new instrument is tested on the telescope.
alt: The spiral galaxy M74, shown in a color composite.
